newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Court hearing to shed light on Port Arthur gunman.
newsitem.headline: Court hearing to shed light on Port Arthur gunman.

text.p: Australia's most notorious mass murderer, Martin Bryant, appears in court on Tuesday for a hearing expected to shed some light on why he went on a shooting rampage which killed 35 people in April.

Bryant, who two weeks ago laughed in court as he confessed to the murders, will appear in Tasmania's Supreme Court for a sentencing hearing expected to last two to three days, separated from survivors in the small public gallery by a sheet of glass.
At least 60 other survivors and relatives of the dead will occupy the jury room, watching the proceedings on a video screen due to the shortage of seats in the small windowless courtroom.

Bryant, 29, arrived at the court building in a prison van with blackened windows early on Tuesday morning, escorted by two police vehicles. Police bomb squad members swarmed over the building and surrounding gardens.

Bryant's lawyer and the prosecution have declined to comment on the arguments they will put to the court, but judge William Cox has said witnesses may be called to testify about Bryant's mental state and all circumstances surrounding the killings.

Bryant overbalanced with laughter during the unnerving November 7 hearing, when he made a surprise decision to reverse his earlier pleas of innocence and confessed to the April 28 massacre at Port Arthur, a popular tourist spot.
He is reported to have changed his plea after his mother, Carleen, visited him in his isolation cell and pleaded with him to spare up to 100 witnesses the trauma of a trial.
Bryant's lawyer, John Avery, had also advised Bryant that no psychiatirc evidence could be obtained to aid a not-guilty plea, The Age newspaper reported this month, quoting unnamed sources.
Bryant, who has been well dressed in a suit and collarless shirt for his two brief court appearances so far, has made no statement to the court other than to enter pleas.
On April 28, a crisp autumn Sunday, Bryant slipped a high-powered rifle from a bag and opened fire at people eating their lunch at a cafe at Port Arthur, a former penal settlement.

Twenty people died in the first hail of bullets, before Bryant moved through the old sandstone ruins at the historic site, gunning down at least 12 other people before holing up in a nearby guesthouse with three others.

Bryant kept police at bay for the night and set fire to the guesthouse in the morning, fleeing the blaze and running into a siege cordon of police. The remains of his final three victims were found later among the charred ruins of the guesthouse.
No motive or explanation for the killings have been given.
